name: Ground beef → plant-based ground alternatives
description: A direct-format swap for recipes that use crumbled or minced meat.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and iron vary substantially by product. TVP and tempeh provide protein; beans can add fiber and iron but may not behave like ground meat. Check labels for iron fortification and sodium.
sensoryMatchNotes: TVP and plant-based grounds can be crumbly; tempeh is firmer and has a distinct texture. Seasoning and moisture affect the result.
recommendationNotes: Choose a product or ingredient based on the texture, flavor, cost, and preparation effort the person wants.

name: Beef steak → seitan or whole-food alternatives
description: Options for replacing a steak-style portion, with different textures and nutrient profiles.
nutritionalNotes: Seitan is protein-rich but contains wheat gluten. Tempeh offers protein and fiber. Mushrooms can provide a savory, substantial texture but are not nutritionally equivalent to steak for protein or iron.
sensoryMatchNotes: Seitan is chewy and tempeh is firm; these options are not identical in texture.
recommendationNotes: For a closer meat-like bite, try seitan or a commercial steak alternative; for a whole-food option, consider tempeh.

name: Beef stew meat → beans or seitan
description: Options for replacing chunks of beef in soups and stews.
nutritionalNotes: Beans provide fiber and plant protein; seitan provides concentrated protein but contains gluten. Cooking time and nutrient content differ from beef.
sensoryMatchNotes: Beans are soft and creamy; seitan is chewy and holds its shape better.
recommendationNotes: Pick based on desired texture: beans for soft spoonable pieces, seitan for a chewier bite.

name: Pork chop → tempeh or seitan
description: Options for replacing a sliced pork portion.
nutritionalNotes: Protein content varies by alternative. Tempeh provides fiber; seitan is protein-rich and contains gluten. Neither should be assumed to match pork micronutrients exactly.
sensoryMatchNotes: Tempeh is firm and slightly nutty; seitan is chewy. Marinades can help adapt flavor.
recommendationNotes: Use a product with a similar thickness and cooking format if a familiar plate-style meal matters.

name: Ground pork → plant-based ground alternatives
description: A minced-texture swap for recipes using ground pork.
nutritionalNotes: Compare protein, iron, sodium, and saturated fat on packaged products. TVP and tempeh offer fiber; nutrition varies by brand.
sensoryMatchNotes: TVP rehydrates into crumbles; plant-based grounds are designed for a similar format; tempeh is more textured.
recommendationNotes: Season to match the intended dish; choose a familiar product format when convenience is important.

name: Bacon → plant-based bacon
description: A smoky, salty, crisp-style alternative for meals that use bacon.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based bacon products vary widely and may be low in protein. Tempeh offers more protein and fiber than many crisp-style substitutes. Check sodium.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial alternatives aim for crispness; tempeh is chewier and less bacon-like.
recommendationNotes: If matching crispness is the priority, try plant-based bacon; if a less processed option is preferred, consider seasoned tempeh.

name: Ham or deli ham → plant-based deli slices
description: A sandwich-friendly swap for sliced ham.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and sodium vary by product. Smoked tofu can provide protein; compare labels for sodium and fortification.
sensoryMatchNotes: Deli slices are designed for a similar thin, flexible format; smoked tofu is firmer and more substantial.
recommendationNotes: Compare taste, texture, sodium, and protein rather than assuming all deli alternatives are nutritionally equivalent.

name: Pork sausage → plant-based sausage
description: A sausage-format replacement for breakfast or other dishes.
nutritionalNotes: Packaged plant-based sausages vary in protein, sodium, and saturated fat. Tempeh provides protein and fiber but is not sausage-like without preparation.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial sausages are closest in shape and cooking behavior; tempeh is firmer and more textured.
recommendationNotes: Choose a plant-based sausage for convenience or tempeh for a whole-food option.

name: Lamb or goat → seitan or legumes
description: Flexible alternatives for recipes using lamb or goat.
nutritionalNotes: Legumes add fiber and plant protein; seitan provides concentrated protein but contains gluten. Nutrient profiles differ from lamb and goat.
sensoryMatchNotes: Seitan is chewy; chickpeas and lentils are softer and work best in dishes where a different texture is acceptable.
recommendationNotes: Match the alternative to the dish rather than treating these ingredients as one-to-one nutritional equivalents.

name: Chicken breast → plant-based chicken or tofu
description: Options for replacing a lean chicken portion.
nutritionalNotes: Protein varies by product. Tofu and seitan provide protein; plant-based chicken may be fortified but can also be high in sodium.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial chicken alternatives mimic a familiar bite; tofu is softer unless pressed or cooked to develop a crust; seitan is chewy.
recommendationNotes: Offer both familiar-format and minimally processed options; compare labels for protein and sodium.

name: Chicken thigh → plant-based chicken or tempeh
description: Options for replacing a richer, darker-meat chicken portion.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and fat vary across alternatives. Tempeh and tofu provide protein and fiber; packaged products vary.
sensoryMatchNotes: Tempeh is firm and textured; tofu is milder; commercial pieces may be closer to chicken in bite.
recommendationNotes: Use marinades and cooking method to create the desired flavor and texture.

name: Ground chicken → plant-based ground alternatives
description: A minced-texture alternative for recipes using ground chicken.
nutritionalNotes: Compare protein, iron, sodium, and saturated fat on packaged alternatives. TVP and tempeh provide fiber.
sensoryMatchNotes: TVP and plant-based grounds can be crumbled; tempeh has a more distinct texture.
recommendationNotes: Choose based on the texture and seasoning needs of the dish.

name: Turkey breast → plant-based deli or chicken alternatives
description: Options for replacing sliced or portioned turkey.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and sodium vary. Smoked tofu provides protein; packaged slices vary in protein and fortification.
sensoryMatchNotes: Deli slices most closely match sandwich use; tofu is firmer and more substantial.
recommendationNotes: For sandwiches, start with deli-style slices; for a plated portion, consider tofu or plant-based chicken.

name: Ground turkey → plant-based ground alternatives
description: A minced-texture swap for ground turkey.
nutritionalNotes: Check product labels for protein, sodium, iron, and saturated fat. TVP and tempeh add fiber.
sensoryMatchNotes: TVP and plant-based grounds create crumbles; tempeh is more textured.
recommendationNotes: Season according to the original dish and choose the texture that feels most familiar.

name: Chicken wings → plant-based chicken pieces
description: A format-based alternative for wing-style dishes.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and sodium vary by brand; compare labels. These products are not guaranteed to match chicken micronutrients.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial pieces and nuggets offer familiar bite-sized formats; coatings can change crispness.
recommendationNotes: Use a plant-based product with a similar shape and preparation method if the format is important.

name: Duck or goose → plant-based poultry-style alternatives
description: Options for replacing poultry in dishes that use duck or goose.
nutritionalNotes: Protein varies. Seitan and tempeh provide protein; tempeh also provides fiber. These are not exact nutrient replacements.
sensoryMatchNotes: Seitan is chewy; tempeh is firm; plant-based chicken products offer a more familiar poultry-style texture.
recommendationNotes: Choose by dish and preferred texture; seasonings can help build a savory profile.

name: Cow’s milk → fortified plant milk
description: A beverage swap for dairy milk.
nutritionalNotes: Fortified soy and pea milks often provide more protein than oat or almond beverages. Calcium and vitamin B12 depend on fortification; shake cartons and check labels.
sensoryMatchNotes: Soy and pea milks are often creamier; oat milk can be naturally sweeter; almond milk is usually lighter.
recommendationNotes: Choose an unsweetened or flavored option according to preference and compare protein, calcium, and B12 fortification.

name: Greek yogurt → high-protein plant yogurt
description: A yogurt swap that prioritizes protein and creamy texture.
nutritionalNotes: Many plant yogurts contain less protein than Greek yogurt. Soy yogurt generally offers more protein than coconut or almond yogurt; fortification varies. If additional protein is needed, compare a separate plant protein food or powder.
sensoryMatchNotes: Plant yogurts vary from thick and creamy to thinner; check consistency and flavor.
recommendationNotes: Compare protein and calcium on the label; select a texture and flavor that is acceptable.

name: Plain yogurt → plant yogurt
description: A simple swap for plain dairy yogurt.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and micronutrient fortification differ by product. Soy yogurt typically has more protein than coconut or almond varieties.
sensoryMatchNotes: Thickness, tang, sweetness, and aftertaste vary widely across brands.
recommendationNotes: Try small containers or different styles to find a preferred texture and flavor; check fortification if using it as a regular substitute.

name: Cheddar cheese → vegan cheddar
description: A cheese-style swap for slices, shreds, or melted applications.
nutritionalNotes: Vegan cheddar products vary in calcium, B12, protein, and saturated fat. Many are lower in protein than dairy cheese; check fortification and labels.
sensoryMatchNotes: Melting, stretch, firmness, and flavor vary by brand and formulation.
recommendationNotes: Choose based on the intended use (melting, sandwich slices, or snacking) and compare calcium/B12 fortification.

name: Mozzarella cheese → vegan mozzarella
description: A cheese-style alternative for melting and mild flavor.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and micronutrient content vary; vegan mozzarella is often not protein-equivalent to dairy mozzarella. Check calcium and B12 fortification.
sensoryMatchNotes: Some products melt and stretch better than others; flavor is often mild.
recommendationNotes: Choose a product designed for the intended use, such as pizza or sandwiches.

name: Parmesan cheese → vegan parmesan
description: A savory, umami-style alternative for grating or sprinkling.
nutritionalNotes: Vegan parmesan and nutritional yeast differ in protein, sodium, and B12. B12 is present only in fortified nutritional yeast or products specifically fortified with it.
sensoryMatchNotes: Nutritional yeast is dry and flaky with a savory flavor; vegan parmesan products vary in texture.
recommendationNotes: Check whether nutritional yeast is B12-fortified; do not assume all brands contain B12.

name: Cream cheese → vegan cream cheese
description: A spreadable alternative for bagels, dips, and toppings.
nutritionalNotes: Vegan cream cheese varies in protein and fortification and may be lower in protein than dairy cream cheese. Silken tofu provides protein but has a different flavor.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial spreads aim for a creamy, spreadable texture; silken tofu is softer and more neutral.
recommendationNotes: Choose based on spreadability and flavor; compare labels if using as a meaningful protein source.

name: Butter → vegan butter
description: A direct cooking and spreading alternative.
nutritionalNotes: Vegan butter products vary in fat composition and saturated fat; they are not intended as a protein or micronutrient replacement.
sensoryMatchNotes: Most products are designed to spread and bake similarly, but performance varies.
recommendationNotes: Choose a product appropriate for baking, cooking, or spreading; check ingredients for allergies.

name: Heavy cream → plant cream
description: A creamy cooking alternative for sauces and soups.
nutritionalNotes: Plant creams vary in fat, calories, and fortification and are not nutritionally equivalent to heavy cream. Coconut-based options have a distinct flavor.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial vegan cream products are designed for cooking; coconut options may add coconut flavor.
recommendationNotes: Use a cooking-specific product when heat stability matters and check whether the flavor suits the dish.

name: Sour cream → vegan sour cream
description: A tangy, creamy topping or ingredient alternative.
nutritionalNotes: Nutrient profiles vary; soy yogurt may provide more protein than some vegan sour creams. Check fortification.
sensoryMatchNotes: Vegan sour cream is formulated for a similar tangy, creamy role; plain soy yogurt may be thinner and less rich.
recommendationNotes: Select by tanginess and thickness; use plain unsweetened soy yogurt where a lighter option works.

name: Cottage cheese → tofu or soy yogurt
description: Alternatives for a soft, protein-containing dairy food.
nutritionalNotes: Tofu and soy yogurt provide plant protein; calcium depends on tofu coagulant and fortification. They are not identical in sodium or texture.
sensoryMatchNotes: Cottage cheese has curds; tofu is smoother or firmer depending on type; soy yogurt is creamy and tangy.
recommendationNotes: Choose the texture first; calcium-set tofu may contribute calcium, but check product information.

name: Whey protein powder → plant protein powder
description: A protein-powder alternative for smoothies or other uses.
nutritionalNotes: Compare protein per serving, amino acid profile, added nutrients, sweeteners, and allergens. Plant powders vary by formulation.
sensoryMatchNotes: Flavor, thickness, and chalkiness vary across products and brands.
recommendationNotes: Choose a powder that tastes acceptable and fits dietary needs; review soy and other allergen information.

name: Casein protein powder → plant protein powder
description: A plant-based protein-powder alternative.
nutritionalNotes: Compare protein per serving and formulation. Plant powders differ in texture, digestion, and amino acid profile; do not assume identical slow-release properties.
sensoryMatchNotes: Plant powders may be thinner or grainier than casein; blending and liquid choice affect texture.
recommendationNotes: Select by taste, protein amount, ingredients, and intended use rather than assuming a one-to-one physiological match.

name: Whole egg → liquid plant-based egg
description: A ready-to-use egg-style alternative for scrambles and some baking uses.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and micronutrients vary by product. Many liquid substitutes are lower in protein than eggs; check B12 and other fortification.
sensoryMatchNotes: Mung-bean-based products can set like scrambled egg; formulations differ in flavor and firmness.
recommendationNotes: Check package guidance because products differ in whether they work for scrambling, baking, or binding.

name: Egg whites → plant-based egg substitute
description: A replacement option for recipes that mainly use egg whites.
nutritionalNotes: Protein varies widely. Some plant-based egg products provide less protein than egg whites; compare labels for the intended serving.
sensoryMatchNotes: Liquid products can mimic pourable egg whites, but foaming and setting behavior may differ.
recommendationNotes: For baking, check whether the product is designed for whipping or binding; not all substitutes perform the same way.

name: Egg yolk → plant-based baking ingredients
description: Options for replacing yolk functions such as richness, binding, or emulsification.
nutritionalNotes: These ingredients serve different culinary functions and are not nutritionally equivalent to egg yolk.
sensoryMatchNotes: Aquafaba is liquid and can foam; ground flax forms a gel; commercial substitutes vary.
recommendationNotes: Choose the ingredient according to the function needed rather than treating them as interchangeable in every recipe.

name: Salmon → plant-based fish alternatives or tofu
description: Options for replacing salmon in meals.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based salmon products vary in protein and omega-3. Tofu provides protein but is not a source of EPA/DHA; algae-derived DHA/EPA can provide these omega-3s separately.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial salmon alternatives aim to mimic flaking and flavor; tofu is firmer and milder.
recommendationNotes: If omega-3 intake is a goal, assess EPA/DHA separately; do not assume a fish-style substitute contains it.

name: Tuna → plant-based tuna alternatives
description: A sandwich- and salad-friendly tuna-style alternative.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based tuna products vary in protein and may be lower than tuna. Chickpeas add fiber and some protein but have a different nutrient profile.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial tuna alternatives aim for a flaky texture; mashed chickpeas are soft and chunky.
recommendationNotes: Choose a product based on the desired texture; chickpeas offer a whole-food option but are not nutritionally identical.

name: Cod or haddock → plant-based white-fish alternatives
description: Options for replacing mild white fish.
nutritionalNotes: Protein and micronutrients vary by product. Tofu provides protein; breaded alternatives may contain more sodium and less protein.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial fillets and fish sticks offer familiar flaky or crisp formats; tofu is denser.
recommendationNotes: Choose by format and compare protein, sodium, and fortification.

name: Sardines or mackerel → plant-based omega-3 sources
description: A plant-based approach to replacing oily fish while considering omega-3 intake.
nutritionalNotes: Walnuts and flax provide ALA, a plant omega-3 that converts only partly to EPA and DHA. Algae-derived EPA/DHA provides these long-chain omega-3s directly. These foods differ in protein, calcium, and other nutrients.
sensoryMatchNotes: Seeds and nuts have a different texture and culinary role from fish; algae oils are usually used as supplements or ingredients.
recommendationNotes: Separate the food swap from the nutrient role: consider algae-derived EPA/DHA if replacing fish as a direct EPA/DHA source.

name: Shrimp → plant-based shrimp alternatives
description: A seafood-style alternative for shrimp dishes.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based shrimp products vary in protein and sodium and may not match shrimp micronutrients. Chickpeas add fiber and some protein but have a different nutrient profile.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial alternatives aim for a springy bite; tofu is firmer and milder.
recommendationNotes: Choose the commercial option for closer format or mushrooms for a whole-food texture; account for protein separately.

name: Crab → plant-based crab alternatives
description: A crab-style alternative for cakes, dips, and other dishes.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based crab products vary; compare protein, sodium, and allergen statements.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial products aim for flaky texture; alternatives may differ in firmness and flavor.
recommendationNotes: Use a product intended for the specific application and check for soy, wheat, or other allergens.

name: Lobster → plant-based seafood alternatives
description: Options for replacing lobster in seafood-style dishes.
nutritionalNotes: These alternatives vary in protein and micronutrients and should not be assumed to match lobster.
sensoryMatchNotes: Seaweed products contribute marine flavor; plant-based shrimp offers a different springy texture.
recommendationNotes: Choose according to flavor and texture goals; assess protein separately if it is important.

name: Scallops → king oyster mushrooms
description: A whole-food option for a seared, scallop-like shape and bite.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based fish-style products and tofu are not nutritionally equivalent replacements for scallops; compare product labels.
sensoryMatchNotes: Plant-based fish-style products and tofu have different textures; select based on the desired preparation.
recommendationNotes: This is primarily a culinary and texture swap; obtain protein from other foods in the meal if needed.

name: Mussels, oysters, or clams → plant-based seafood alternatives
description: Plant-based options for shellfish-style dishes.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based seafood alternatives are not nutritionally equivalent to shellfish, particularly for vitamin B12, iron, zinc, and protein. Nutrient content varies.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial alternatives vary in briny flavor and texture.
recommendationNotes: Do not assume seaweed or mushrooms replace shellfish micronutrients; review B12, iron, and zinc intake separately.

name: Squid or octopus → king oyster mushrooms
description: A mushroom-based option for chewy, seafood-style preparations.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based seafood alternatives provide a different nutrient profile and are not necessarily protein-equivalent replacements for squid or octopus.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial alternatives and tofu have different textures; choose based on the preparation and preferred bite.
recommendationNotes: Use as a culinary swap and account for protein separately if needed.

name: Animal-based protein in a meal → legumes or soy foods
description: A flexible swap when the priority is adding plant protein rather than reproducing a specific meat texture.
nutritionalNotes: Legumes and soy foods provide plant protein and fiber; iron content and absorption differ from meat. Pairing plant iron sources with vitamin-C-rich foods can support absorption.
sensoryMatchNotes: Beans and lentils are soft; tofu is mild and can be firm; tempeh is chewy and textured.
recommendationNotes: Ask which foods the person already eats and which textures they prefer before recommending a specific option.

name: Animal-based meatballs → plant-based meatballs
description: A shape- and format-matched swap for meatballs.
nutritionalNotes: Packaged plant-based meatballs vary in protein, sodium, and saturated fat. TVP and tempeh provide protein and fiber but require shaping and seasoning.
sensoryMatchNotes: Commercial meatballs are closest in shape; TVP and tempeh mixtures have a more variable texture.
recommendationNotes: Use a ready-made product for convenience or a base ingredient when the person wants to prepare their own.

name: Beef burger patty → plant-based burger patty
description: A burger-format swap.
nutritionalNotes: Plant-based burger nutrition varies widely. Compare protein, iron fortification, sodium, and saturated fat across products.
sensoryMatchNotes: Products vary in juiciness, firmness, and browning; cooking instructions matter.
recommendationNotes: Choose by taste and texture preference and compare nutrition labels rather than assuming all patties are equivalent.

name: Chicken nuggets → plant-based nuggets
description: A familiar bite-sized alternative.
nutritionalNotes: Protein, sodium, and fiber vary by brand; breaded products may be lower in protein than unbreaded options.
sensoryMatchNotes: Designed to provide a familiar crisp coating and bite; brands vary.
recommendationNotes: A format-matched option can reduce the number of changes made at once; check allergen information.
